articles.body: NEW DELHI: BJP leader and former Union minister Ravneet Singh Bittu shared videos on X showing his detention by police after he protested with eggs and tomatoes as Punjab Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann's cavalcade passed through Ludhiana.In the footage, Bittu could be heard saying, "throw, throw!" as police detained him. The video was posted with the caption, "Love to Bhagwant Mann from Punjabis."Bittu was detained by Ludhiana Police and taken to an undisclosed location.He stepped up his criticism of Punjab Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann, accusing the state government of failing to act against those allegedly involved in the attack on his convoy and the BJP's 'Nasha Mukt Punjab Yatra'.Bittu alleged that the attack was linked to the drug trade in the state and claimed that no action had been taken against those responsible. He also challenged Mann to confront him directly, saying, "If Bhagwant Mann had the guts, he would have faced me. Today, the Chief Minister is making a narrow escape.""You have addicted all of Punjab to drugs. You are getting people attacked because you are colluding with drug traffickers. That is why you orchestrated an attack on me and the BJP yatra yesterday. I would not have had to come here today if action had been taken against those goons. However, no action was taken against them because they are the biggest drug lords," he added.He also urged the Sikh community's leadership to lodge a formal complaint over the alleged disruption of devotees travelling during the Viah Purab celebrations of Guru Nanak Dev Ji. Referring to the throwing of eggs on the road, he said, "Today, I want to appeal to Jathedar Sahib that a formal complaint be lodged.""The Viah Purab of Guru Nanak Dev Ji is being celebrated. People were laying down mats on the road; they were sweeping it clean so that no one would step on anything unclean or get a speck of dirt on them. The entire Sangat was proceeding to pay obeisance, but it was disrupted. Just imagine, eggs were thrown at the very spot on the road where the Sangat was traveling. I urge Jathedar Sahib to ensure a formal complaint is lodged," he said.He further appealed for those responsible to be removed from the Sikh community, saying, "Those responsible for this should be expelled from the Panth (Sikh community).""If the Chief Minister has the guts, let him come himself and face me. If we were to start doing the same thing, you would not be able to set foot in any state. The windows of all my vehicles were smashed yesterday; I only survived because I was in a bulletproof car," Bittu said.The development came a day after Bittu alleged that his cavalcade was attacked while he was travelling to Pathankot to attend a BJP yatra.He accused the AAP government of turning into a “gangster party” and alleged that police failed to take action during the incident."There was an attack on me. AAP has become a gangster party. If someone who has security protection is attacked by 200 people, Shery Kalsi and Joban were heading this," Bittu had said."DSP, SP, were present there. Just before this happened, the police got our convoy to slow down and then helped the perpetrators run away. The police were present there at the time. Those people again came to attack a second time. One, Anmol Randhawa was caught by us. Their thought was to scare a top leader so that it would result in spreading fear in the other BJP leaders. The DGP and the CM should be ashamed," he added.Bittu alleged that protesters surrounded his convoy, threatened to attack those inside and damaged the windows of the vehicles. He also claimed that some of the protesters were carrying weapons.The BJP's 'Nasha Mukt Punjab Yatra' was launched across the state on Friday as part of the party's campaign to raise awareness about the drug menace. Bittu was travelling to Pathankot to participate in the campaign when he alleged that his convoy was attacked by around 500 people.BJP MP Raghav Chadha alleged that the Aam Aadmi Party was "scared" and attempting to target Bittu following the alleged attack on his cavalcade.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.body: A Sri Lankan opposition lawmaker on Saturday urged President Anura Kumara Dissanayake to seek Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s intervention in the case of a young Sri Lankan Tamil facing judicial proceedings in Saudi Arabia.In making the appeal, Mano Ganesan, a leader of the Tamil Progressive Alliance, cited PM Modi’s “close ties” with Saudi Crown Prince and Prime Minister Mohammed bin Salman.“I urge President @anuradisanayake to bring #Anojan_Sivarasa’s desperate plight to the urgent attention of your friend, recipient of ‘SriLanka Rathna’ Prime Minister Narendra Modi,” Ganesan wrote on X.“Given PM Modi’s close ties with Saudi Prime Minister and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, I appeal to you to ask PM Modi to personally intervene with Crown Prince Salman and seek a humanitarian resolution for Anojan,” he added.The appeal concerns Sri Lankan national Anojan Sivarasa, whose family has claimed that he was sentenced to death in Saudi Arabia over a social media post allegedly amounting to blasphemy.Sri Lanka’s foreign ministry, however, has not confirmed that Sivarasa has been sentenced to death.Sivarasa, a minority Tamil from Sri Lanka’s Eastern Province, is a resident of Natpittimunai in Kalmunai. He travelled to Saudi Arabia for employment nine months ago.The Sri Lankan ministry of foreign affairs on Friday confirmed that it remains engaged with Saudi authorities over the case.“The ministry remains engaged with the relevant Saudi authorities through diplomatic channels and is taking appropriate steps to safeguard Mr. Anojan Sivarasa’s interests and provide him with all possible assistance,” it said.Sivarasa was initially sentenced to five years in prison and fined three million Saudi riyals after being found guilty of posting social media content deemed insulting to a religion.According to the report, his lawyer later verbally informed the Sri Lankan Embassy in Riyadh that the sentence had reportedly been enhanced to capital punishment.The embassy, however, is awaiting the formal written judgment from Saudi judicial authorities before confirming the development.The lawyer has also informed the embassy that the judgment could be appealed before Saudi Arabia’s Supreme Court within one month. The embassy, in consultation with the ministry, is taking steps to pursue the appeal in coordination with Sivarasa’s family.Sri Lankan Tamils account for around 12-13% of the island nation’s population of more than 20 million and are mainly concentrated in the Northern and Eastern provinces.(With PTI inputs)Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.body:
A column of black smoke has been seen near Riyadh's international airport hours after air raid alerts were issued in the Saudi capital.

It was the first time residents had been given an alert and urged to stay indoors since a recent escalation in the conflict with Iran-backed Houthi militants in neighbouring Yemen.

A number of apparent explosions were heard in the capital and major problems were reported at King Khalid International Airport, with the tracking website FlightRadar24 reporting delays and cancellations earlier in the day .

One report suggested a fuel tank had been set on fire near the airport. There has been no official comment from Saudi authorities.

An AFP news agency journalist reported that firefighters could be seen trying to extinguish the flames of a burnt-out fuel tank belonging to state oil and gas company Aramco.

The Saudi Civil Defence had sent out phone alerts overnight warning of potential danger in Riyadh and other regions, before issuing an all-clear on Saturday morning.

Residents told AFP on condition of anonymity that they had heard what sounded like a round of explosions echoing through the city after the alerts.

"I heard the alarm, then my windows shook," said a resident of northern Riyadh, 27. "It was definitely scary. I was not expecting this."

On Friday, the Houthis announced that they had thwarted Saudi attacks on the Yemeni capital Sanaa which they said bore the hallmarks of an Islamic State operation.

Houthi military spokesman Yahya al-Sarea said Saudi Arabia had carried out 300 strikes across Yemen during the past week.

He warned the reported attacks on Sanaa would "not go unanswered".

The Houthis are locked in a civil war with Yemen's internationally recognised government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia.

They have attacked targets inside Saudi Arabia on several occasions in recent months, and said this week that they were responsible for downing a Saudi fighter jet over Yemen.

According to an unconfirmed report from AFP, quoting military sources on both sides of Yemen's civil war, fighting between the Houthis and Saudi-backed government forces claimed 48 lives on Saturday.

The Houthis said 31 of their fighters had been killed while government sources said their side had lost 17 soldiers, according to the news agency.

On Friday, the International Organization for Migration, a UN body, reported that the number of people displaced as a result of recent fighting had passed 104,796 .

The Houthis recently seized control of the strategic port city of Mokha and Perim Island, a gateway to a key shipping route used by the Gulf state to export to Asia and Europe.

The group said the naval blockade was in retaliation for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in Houthi-controlled north-western Yemen.

Saudi vessels have relied on that stretch of the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz.

On Friday, investment banking giant JP Morgan said it was struggling to predict how oil prices would be impacted by the war, telling investors in a rare note that "we simply don't know how to model the endgame".

articles.title: Fashion executive resigns days after restraining PETA protesters at New York runway show
articles.summary: Steven Kolb, who is well known and respected in the New York fashion world, earlier apologized for his actions.
articles.body: NEW YORK — The longtime chief executive of the Council of Fashion Designers of America announced Friday that he is stepping down, days after he was filmed physically restraining two protesters during an altercation at a New York runway show. “I am enormously proud of what we have built together and believe this is the right moment for both me and the organization to begin a new chapter,” Steven Kolb said in a statement. Kolb is stepping down after two decades leading the council, which is known as the fashion industry’s main trade organization. The incident Sunday involved the top fashion executive forcibly restraining two employees of People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals and putting his hands over their mouths at the runway show for Cos, a brand owned by H&M. It quickly stunned many in the fashion world. Kolb, who is well known and respected in the New York fashion world, earlier apologized for his actions. He also had announced he was taking a leave from his job pending an investigation. CFDA described Kolb as a “dedicated leader and tireless champion of American fashion.” “We respect Steven’s decision to step down and are grateful for his many years of leadership and service to the CFDA and our industry,” the association said in a statement on social media. Moira Colley, senior director of media relations for PETA in New York, said earlier in the week that the group planned to meet with Kolb to discuss ending the use of wool and animal skins in clothing. The organization had initially planned on filing a police report against Kolb, but changed course after visiting police and consulting attorneys. PETA issued a statement after Kolb’s announcement Friday, saying the group still planned to meet with him and “hopefully others in the industry will meet and take meaningful steps to stop this epidemic of cruelty to animals.” The group has also recognized Kolb’s previous involvement in getting fur banned from runway shows on the CFDA schedule. Andrija Barak had been trying to disrupt the runway show on Sunday, calling out slogans about the use of wool. In the video, Kolb is seen covering her mouth with his hands and restraining her with both his arms and a leg over her body as he seeks to let the show continue. articles.title: Meet Everett Leigh, the 16-year-old California pianist who organised 50+ benefit concerts, raised $70,000 and helped generate another $2 million for foster youth
articles.summary: US News: For Everett, the piano has become more than a stage for showcasing musical talent. The California teenager has used concerts, competitions, and his gr.
articles.body: For Everett, the piano has become more than a stage for showcasing musical talent. The California teenager has used concerts, competitions, and his growing network in the classical music world to raise money and awareness for children facing difficult circumstances. Now 16, Leigh is the founder of EverEverest, a nonprofit focused on supporting foster and underserved youth through educational programmes, mentorship and supplies. His recent recognition as one of the 2026 Barron Prize for Young Heroes winners has brought renewed attention to his work. The Barron Prize describes Leigh as a young concert pianist who has organised more than 50 benefit concerts, raising $70,000 for foster youth. It also credits him with helping raise an additional $2 million for Foster Love, a major US nonprofit serving children in foster care.A popular pianistHis work has developed alongside an unusually busy musical career. Leigh began studying piano under Professor Ethan Dong at the age of nine. By his mid-teens, he had accumulated more than 50 international competition victories, according to his Steinway profile and several competition organisations. His honours include the Pianist of the Year title at the AD LIBITUM Warsaw International Piano Competition, first-place finishes at the SoCal Philharmonic Young Artists Concerto Competition and victories at international competitions in Hong Kong, Vienna and elsewhere.He has also performed as a soloist with orchestras including the Pacific Symphony, San Diego Symphony, Santa Barbara Symphony and SoCal Philharmonic. His performances have taken him to venues including Carnegie Hall and Walt Disney Concert Hall.He has won three consecutive Presidential Gold Volunteer Service Awards alongside special recognitions from the U.S. Congress. Everett is the sole Junior Piano Soloist appointed by the United Nations, representing UNITAR, with his performance at the "Piano Recital Recording Concert for Refugees" at the UN Plaza featured in a documentary produced by the UN.But his work away from the concert stage has become an equally important part of his story.A changemakerThrough EverEverest, Leigh has helped organise performances and other events aimed at directing resources towards children who need support. The organisation describes itself as a social enterprise that uses the talents of its members and volunteers, from musicians organising benefit concerts to athletes hosting fundraising events. As for Everett, he believes that "opportunity should be a right, not a privilege."One of the biggest parts of that effort has involved Foster Love. Leigh has performed at the organisation's fundraising gala, including alongside America's Got Talent winner Richard Goodall. EverEverest says the gala raised more than $1 million for foster children, while the 2026 Barron Prize announcement credits Leigh's involvement with helping generate $2 million for Foster Love.Best of both worldsHis musical journey has continued to expand in 2026. Sempre Musick named Leigh a Grand Prix winner in its 2026 Concerto Competition. The award gives him an opportunity to perform with the New Hampshire Philharmonic Orchestra during the 2026-27 season. The competition's profile again notes his more than 50 international competition victories and his work with EverEverest.He was also selected as one of the finalists in the 2026 Vancouver Piano Sessions Concerto Competition. In August, he performed the third movement of Rachmaninoff's Piano Concerto No. 3 with the Vancouver Metropolitan Orchestra at the competition's gala concert.Leigh's activities extend beyond conventional classical performance. He has explored the intersection of music, artificial intelligence, engineering and neuroscience through BioMus, a project that investigates ways brain signals and facial movements can be translated into musical expression. His Steinway profile also identifies him as a Young Steinway Artist and notes his appointment as a Junior Piano Soloist representing UNITAR, the UN Institute for Training and Research.For Leigh, however, the growing list of awards and performances appears to be only one part of what he wants music to accomplish. His benefit concerts have given him a way to connect his musical ambitions with a cause beyond the concert hall, turning performances into fundraising opportunities for children in foster care.At 16, he is therefore building two careers in parallel: one as a highly competitive young classical pianist, and another as a youth philanthropist using the reach of music to support children who need it.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: BJP promise in its coastal bastion: Why DK Shivakumar put Tulu at centre in Mangaluru
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Karnataka chief minister DK Shivakumar on Friday announced that Tulu, spoken in the state's Dakshina Kannada and Udupi districts, would be .
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Karnataka chief minister DK Shivakumar on Friday announced that Tulu, spoken in the state's Dakshina Kannada and Udupi districts, would be recognised as an additional administrative language in the region, fulfilling a long-standing demand."Today, we have decided to make Tulu applicable to Udupi and Dakshina Kannada districts and declare it the state’s second additional administrative language," Shivakumar told reporters after a marathon cabinet meeting in Mangaluru.According to a cabinet note shared by the chief minister’s office, Tulu would be Karnataka’s "second additional administrative language" in Dakshina Kannada and Udupi.The 2011 national census recorded more than 18 lakh native Tulu speakers in Karnataka, whose population was recorded at over six crore at the time. Kannada is the state's most-widely spoken and its primary official language.This was also the first time a cabinet meeting was held in Mangaluru and not in Bengaluru.Eye on BJP's coastal bastionThe political significance of Shivakumar taking his cabinet to Mangaluru becomes clearer against the BJP's electoral dominance in the region.Coastal Karnataka, particularly Dakshina Kannada and Udupi, has long been one of the BJP's strongest pockets in the state. In the 2023 Karnataka assembly election, BJP won 11 of the 13 seats across the two districts, taking all five seats in Udupi and six of the eight in Dakshina Kannada. The Congress won only two constituencies.This was despite Congress sweeping to power across Karnataka with 135 seats, against 66 for the BJP.The BJP's hold remained intact in the 2024 Lok Sabha election. It won both parliamentary seats covering the region, with Brijesh Chowta defeating Congress's Padmaraj R by over 64,000 votes in Dakshina Kannada. Kota Srinivas Poojary won Udupi-Chikkamagaluru by more than 2.5 lakh votes.The BJP responded to the Tulu announcement by alleging that Shivakumar was "peddling soft Hindutva to make a dent in the BJP’s vote bank.""Shivakumar has never made any secret of his firm belief in Hinduism and frequently visits temples, performs rituals publicly and quotes scriptures. He is now peddling soft Hindutva. This was also evident from his rendition of 'Namaste Sada Vatsale' inside the Karnataka assembly," a BJP leader told PTI, referring to an August 2025 incident in which Shivakumar sang a few lines of the RSS anthem.The RSS is the BJP's ideological mentor.But there is a political twist to the Tulu issue itself. The BJP had previously taken up the demand while in power in Karnataka.In January 2023, the then BJP government led by Basavaraj Bommai constituted a committee to examine granting Tulu the status of a second official language in the state, months before the assembly election.More than just TuluSignificantly, Shivakumar’s announcements went beyond granting Tulu the status of a second administrative language.The Cabinet meeting in Mangaluru marked the Shivakumar government’s first meeting outside Bengaluru, the state capital. Shivakumar claimed the move was intended to recognise the region’s contribution and address its development needs.The chief minister added that a draft notification would soon be issued to invite public feedback on renaming the Dakshina Kannada district to Mangaluru district.He also announced a host of policies for the coastal Karnataka region, introducing a dedicated tourism policy for the coastal areas to treats tourism projects as infrastructure initiatives while offering investors special incentives and extended loan repayment windows.Additionally, the government approved the Karnataka Marine Biotechnology Policy, 2026-31, which paves the way for upgrading the existing fisheries college into the Fisheries, Marine and Blue Economy University and expanding its student intake from 60 to 200 seats.Beyond these policies, the administration unveiled new urban development planning, fisheries sector incentives, and major financial allocations totaling around Rs 32,611 crore—split evenly between rural development and regional growth for Mangaluru, Udupi, and the coastal region.The announcements further included plans to hold decentralised Cabinet meetings across 10 to 12 locations in the state over the next 15 months and the sanctioning of a new medical college worth approximately Rs 450 crore for the region.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: For Palestinian aid groups, Macklemore’s $1M pledge after Ed Sheeran drama brings attention to ongoing suffering
articles.summary: For the Palestinian relief nonprofits behind a $1 million pledge from rapper Macklemore, the Grammy winner’s latest contributions offer more than just money.
articles.body: For the Palestinian relief nonprofits behind a $1 million pledge from rapper Macklemore, the Grammy winner’s latest contributions offer more than just money. Macklemore committed to donate his net earnings from Ed Sheeran’s Loop Tour after he was dropped for making pro-Palestinian comments onstage at New Jersey’s MetLife Stadium. The goal, he wrote in a Wednesday post on social media, was to “bring the conversation back to where it belongs” — the Palestinian people — after a 48-hour period that saw four supporting acts quit in solidarity and confusion over who held responsibility for the decision. The six donation recipients included Medical Aid for Palestinians, Palestine Children’s Relief Fund and the U.N. agency for Palestinian refugees, UNRWA. In addition to the funding windfall, their leaders welcomed the renewed public awareness of the perilous living conditions faced by the Palestinian people they treat regularly. “Even if you don’t see bombs falling every night, the rubble is still there,” said Alicia Phillips Mandaville, the acting CEO of Anera, another beneficiary. “And the traumatized children are still traumatized.” Attention on continued pleas for help Tareq Hailat, the director of strategic engagement at Palestine Children’s Relief Fund, said his phone rings “all the time” with calls from people in Gaza “bleeding and asking for help.” “There are children dying every single day. There’s our team that is constantly in danger on the ground every single day. There’s people we have to feed,” he said. “So to have this attention on it is incredible.” Israeli operations have killed more than 1,000 Palestinians since a fragile ceasefire took effect last October. Hundreds of thousands of Palestinians struggle to get healthcare in the West Bank. Palestinians say water shortages persist. The world’s leading authority on food insecurity warned in July that most Gaza families still weren’t getting nearly enough to eat even as Israel allowed more aid. The Palestinian Children’s Relief Fund medically evacuates children who can’t get the care they need because of crumbling healthcare infrastructure and flies outside physicians in to treat others inside Gaza. The nonprofit will put its share of Macklemore’s gift into an unrestricted fund, according to Hailat. The donation allows leaders to more fluidly direct money based on the evolving circumstances inside Gaza. Anera — a humanitarian aid group working in Palestine, Lebanon and Jordan — noted its donation also came with no requirements for how to use the money. Mandaville said that flexibility is important when “the way people live” and “the rules we work inside” change on a monthly basis. “If there’s flooding again this year like there was last year, we can deal with that. If there is an acute hunger crisis again, like there has been in the past, we can meet that,” she said. “We can buy more blankets because people want their grandparents to be warm at night.” Macklemore has long supported Palestinians This week’s gift wasn’t the first time Macklemore has donated to some of the recipients. The rapper has long advocated for Palestinians. He previously pledged the proceeds and streaming royalties from his protest anthems “Hind’s Hall” and “Hind’s Hall 2” to UNRWA. More than $509,000 in support has come through those royalties, according to UNRWA USA CEO Mara Kronenfeld. “He has been contributing to saving probably hundreds of thousands of lives in Gaza through his contributions already,” she said. This latest donation is already catalyzing more gifts. Ms. Rachel, a YouTube star and music teacher, announced Thursday that she would donate $1 million to the Palestinian Children’s Relief Fund and called on others to match the gift. New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft — whose Kraft Group also owns Gillette Stadium, where Sheeran is scheduled to perform later this month — said in a Wednesday Instagram post that he would match Sheeran’s own $2 million donation for aid “in the region.” Macklemore has said his removal was the result of an effort led by Kraft. The post did not specify the gift’s recipients. Others inspired to donate Everyday donors appear to be joining efforts like Ms. Rachel’s. Online progressive influencers have helped raise more than $72,000 more for the Palestinian Children’s Relief Fund. Anera reported that the donations it received Wednesday through social media platforms were more than triple this month’s daily average. The nonprofit has also gained more than 8,000 followers since Macklemore tagged its account in his post. Mandaville hopes that exposure will introduce new, younger audiences to the nonprofit’s work. “I would guess that our traditional donor does not know the lyrics to ‘Thrift Shop,”’ she said, referencing Macklemore’s breakout 2012 hit. UNRWA USA’s Kronenfeld said the spike reflects an existing trend. Her organization has gained 203,000 donors since October 2023, she said, allowing them to send more than $117 million. “The contributions keep coming in because Americans care,” she said. “It will increase that much more with Macklemore’s extremely humane gesture.”

articles.title: Hackers aren’t just stealing data anymore, they’re stealing your AI access
articles.summary: Tech News News: It sounds absurd: someone breaks into your system, and instead of emptying your database, they start making you pay for their AI.But that is increasin.
articles.body: It sounds absurd: someone breaks into your system, and instead of emptying your database, they start making you pay for their AI.But that is increasingly the point.A stolen AI credential can give an attacker more than access to a company. It can give them computing power that the company has already paid for.Attackers are increasingly stealing API keys, login sessions and other credentials that provide access to AI services, using them to run their own workloads, resell the access or hide behind legitimate customer accounts. The target is no longer necessarily the data sitting inside an organisation. In some cases, it is the AI access itself.Anthropic’s September 2026 threat report describes an emerging criminal economy built around stolen AI access. Attackers are harvesting credentials from code repositories, mobile applications, websites, Docker containers, chatbots and other places where companies accidentally expose them. Those credentials can then be resold, used in further attacks, or simply used to run AI workloads at the legitimate customer’s expense.The economics are simple: one stolen key can deliver three things - loot, compute and cover.Loot - because stolen AI credentials can be resold.Compute - because someone else can foot the bill for the workload.Cover - because the activity can look like it is coming from a legitimate customer.CrowdStrike's 2026 Threat Hunting Report has observed a similar shift. In one campaign, attackers abusing corporate AI access generated nearly 200,000 API requests in an initial two-minute flood, using the victim's AI resources rather than simply stealing information from the account.AI access is becoming something criminals can sellAn API key is a string of characters that works like a digital pass. It allows an application to use an online service without a person having to log in each time. When linked to an AI service, that key can allow software to send requests to an AI model.A session token serves a similar purpose. It is a digital proof that a user has already logged in and can allow continued access to an account.If criminals steal either, they may not need the victim's password. They may be able to use the existing access instead.Anand Venkatraman, Partner, Deloitte India, said this represents a change in how stolen credentials are viewed.“API keys and session tokens have emerged as a new class of high-value digital assets. Historically, stolen credentials were a means to access networks, applications, or data. Today, the credential itself is often the target.”The reason is simple. A working AI credential can already have an economic value.“A live API key linked to a funded enterprise AI account is a monetizable asset that can be resold or abused directly, much like cloud credentials became valuable commodities once cloud compute gained economic value,” Venkatraman said.In other words, criminals do not necessarily need to steal what an AI service has generated. They can steal the ability to use the service in the first place.Anthropic says one hacktivist campaign ran for an entire month using stolen API keys. In another case, suspected ShinyHunters affiliates stole AI keys during an intrusion and switched their own attack workloads onto those keys.The theft is also becoming industrialised.One criminal pipeline downloaded 1.8 million Android APKs, decompiled them and searched them for hardcoded secrets. A separate harvesting operation collected GitHub personal access tokens. The stolen credentials were then validated and fed into criminal operations.Another group went after users themselves by pretending to sell cheap access to frontier AI models. Victims who installed what appeared to be AI software instead handed over credentials and authenticated session tokens. The stolen access was then sold onward to other AI resellers.And the target is not limited to ordinary AI users.Criminals can make the victim pay for their AI useAI services are generally paid for based on usage. The more a customer uses a model, the more computing resources are consumed and, depending on the service, the larger the bill can become.This creates an opportunity for attackers.They can take a stolen credential and use the victim's account to run their own AI workloads. This is sometimes referred to as LLMJacking, where criminals hijack access to an AI model and use the victim's computing resources.CrowdStrike said it observed financially motivated criminals abusing corporate large language model, or LLM, access for LLMJacking and cost harvesting. In one campaign, attackers sent nearly 200,000 API requests in an initial two-minute flood.CrowdStrike describes cloud resource hijacking as the unauthorised use of a victim's computing resources after an account is compromised. The same approach can be used for cryptocurrency mining or AI workloads, with the victim effectively providing the computing power and paying the associated cost.Venkatraman said the economics are similar to earlier forms of cybercrime.“The move from data theft to access theft reflects a natural evolution of cybercrime. Underground markets have progressed from selling VPN and RDP access to cloud credentials, and now AI platform access.”The attraction is that a stolen AI account may already have a payment method, an established usage history and access to models that could otherwise be expensive to use.A legitimate account can also provide coverThere is another advantage for criminals. Activity carried out using a legitimate customer's account can be harder to distinguish from normal usage.“A stolen AI credential isn't just reusable, it's a paid-for gateway: the attacker inherits legitimate compute quota and model access under someone else's billing and identity, making the activity far harder to flag than a conventional stolen password,” said Saurabh Sharma, security researcher, Global Research and Analysis Team (GReAT), Kaspersky.Venkatraman identified three reasons stolen AI credentials are attractive: they can be resold, they provide access to paid computing resources and they allow criminals to operate through a legitimate customer's account.This means an attacker does not always have to create a new account or find a way to pay for AI services. The victim's existing access can do that work.Developers are leaving credentials in places criminals can searchThe growing value of AI credentials is also changing what criminals look for when searching the internet.Anthropic said attackers have been searching public code repositories, mobile applications, container images and websites for API keys and session tokens. In one case documented by the company, an attacker stole AI API keys from an enterprise software vendor and subsequently used one of those keys for secondary attacks against other organisations.The problem often starts with something as straightforward as a developer accidentally leaving a key inside software code.Venkatraman said common sources include “Hardcoded keys committed to repositories and exposed through forks or misconfigured CI/CD pipelines”, credentials embedded inside mobile applications, secrets included in container images and tokens exposed through client-side JavaScript.A container image is essentially a packaged version of software that can be moved between computers or cloud services. If a secret is accidentally included in that package, anyone who obtains it may also obtain the credential.Kaspersky has seen similar activity in developer tools. Sharma cited the 2025 singularity incident, in which attackers stole a package-publishing token and used it to push malicious npm packages designed to steal secrets from Claude Code, Gemini CLI and Amazon Q CLI.CrowdStrike also found attackers targeting software development environments, package registries and container registries. It said npm accounted for 87% of malicious software registry threats in the first half of 2026.AI is adding more links to the supply chainThe term AI supply chain can sound abstract, but the idea is relatively simple. Companies increasingly connect AI services to their software, customer support systems, internal databases and automated assistants. Each connection needs some form of permission or credential.That creates more places where access can be exposed or stolen.AI agents are making this network wider. An AI agent is software that can carry out tasks on behalf of a user, rather than simply responding to a question. Such agents can be connected to email, messaging, calendars, company databases and other services.Sharma said this is creating more potential routes into an organisation.“Absolutely every new integration point is a new credential to protect. We've flagged that AI agents are frequently connected to email, messaging, task-management systems, knowledge bases and MCP servers, meaning a malicious instruction or a credential leak can now originate from virtually any source the agent processes automatically.”For companies, that means protecting an AI system is no longer only about securing the model itself. The credentials that connect the model to other services can become targets too.Venkatraman said this is particularly relevant for Indian enterprises because AI deployments can also create new compliance responsibilities.“This trend resembles the evolution from "shadow IT" to "shadow cloud" and now "shadow AI." For Indian enterprises, governance challenges are amplified by requirements such as RBI outsourcing guidelines, CERT-In incident reporting obligations, and the DPDP framework.”He said organisations should treat AI credentials with the same level of care as other privileged access, including limiting what each credential can do, regularly replacing credentials, monitoring their use and including them in incident response plans.Get the latest technology news and updates. articles.title: Department of State approves potential $2.6 billion military air defense equipment sale to Ukraine
articles.summary: The State Department approved a potential $2.6 billion air defense equipment sale to Ukraine Friday as its conflict with Russia resumed following trilateral talks with U.S. special envoys. In a congressional notification, the State Department wrote that the Ukrainian government requested S-300 Clone missiles, GAM-67 missiles, Range-Extended Air Defense Laser Guided Rocket missile systems, counter-drone…
articles.body:
The State Department approved a potential $2.6 billion air defense equipment sale to Ukraine Friday as its conflict with Russia resumed following trilateral talks with U.S. special envoys.

In a congressional notification , the State Department wrote that the Ukrainian government requested S-300 Clone missiles, GAM-67 missiles, Range-Extended Air Defense Laser Guided Rocket missile systems, counter-drone radars and other related elements of logistics and program support.

The department continued that “if the proposed purchase is concluded, Ukraine would finance it using a combination of European contributions and U.S. Foreign Military Financing appropriated during the prior Administration.”

“The FMF [Foreign Military Sale] will be counted as a U.S. capital contribution to the Ukraine Reconstruction Investment Fund via a 1:1 reimbursement,” the agency stated.

The U.S. Embassy in Kyiv similarly posted on social media that the potential sale would “improve Ukraine’s capability to meet current and future threats” by “equipping it to conduct self-defense and regional security missions with a more robust air defense capability.”

President Trump also signed the Russia sanctions into effect Friday, which authorizes further sanctions and tariffs against Russia.

The bill — championed and named after late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.) — called for the president to calls for the president to impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on the top five purchasers of Russian energy, or on countries helping Russia evade sanctions — even extending current sanctions on Iran

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called the Russia sanctions bill “critically important” for his country.

“The best way to honor Lindsey’s memory will be to implement the provisions of this law fully and swiftly,” Zelensky said. “And the best reward for everyone helping us put pressure on Russia to end its war will be peace.”

The actions follow attempted trilateral peace talks between Moscow, Kyiv and U.S. special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law. Witkoff said the U.S. is confident that talks will result in a “ good resolution ” to the conflict after a weekend-long ceasefire was called for their visit.

The conflict, however, has reignited since peace talks, with Russia launching strikes against targets in Kyiv and other major cities earlier this week, according to Ukraine’s Defense Ministry . European Union Ambassador to Ukraine Katarina Mathernova confirmed that at least two people were killed and 10 injured in the strikes.

Zelensky, speaking at a press conference, said his country had pleaded to the U.S. and other allies to provide critical air defenses — particularly Patriot interceptors — to counter Russian ballistic missiles before the winter.

articles.title: Oxfordshire County Council issues climate action grants
articles.summary: The funds will support projects including tree-planting, growing food and tackling climate anxiety.
articles.body:
More than 50 community projects will receive climate action grants after a summer of heatwaves.

Oxfordshire County Council awarded funding to help kickstart 54 projects tackling the impacts of extreme weather.

The grants range from £85 to £3,000 and will be used by 31 Oxfordshire organisations exploring climate action in the face of high temperatures, floods, droughts and storms.

The funds are part of an expanded community resilience grants programme, administered by Community Action Groups Oxfordshire (CAG) and funded by £44,724 from Oxfordshire County Council.

This year saw a significant increase in grants awarded, with 11 groups receiving a total of £12,000 in 2025.

The grants will go towards projects exploring practical solutions including planting trees, growing food and harvesting rainwater, the council said.

Projects will also look at the impacts extreme weather has on health and wellbeing, taking action like creating cooler community spaces, making homes more comfortable during heatwaves and tackling climate anxiety.

Oxfordshire County Council's cabinet member for environment and economy, Laura Gordon, said: "The increase in funding allocated for these grants this year shows how important we believe it is to support communities in carrying out these projects. They are the experts and know their own areas better than anyone.

"This summer's heatwaves were not one-off occurrences, but the new reality for the UK and we all need to adapt."

Among the grant recipients was Cherwell Collective, which successfully applied in all three categories – heat-safe homes, community resilience and climate anxiety.

Programme manager Victoria Russell said: "The funds are going to help us tackle climate anxiety within Oxfordshire."

articles.title: Jackson's Coppice nature reserve to 'double in size'
articles.summary: Staffordshire Wildlife Trust acquires an area of wet woodland, marsh and pastureland due to the will.
articles.body:
A nature reserve will double in size due to a generous gift left in a will, a wildlife trust has said.

The donation has secured more land at Jackson's Coppice and Marsh Nature Reserve near Eccleshall, Staffordshire.

An area of wet woodland and marsh has been acquired alongside pastureland south of the River Sow. Public footpaths and a scheme to slow the flow of the river in heavy rainfall are being planned.

"This is fantastic news for wildlife and a wonderful example of how gifts in wills can create lasting change for nature," Jeff Sim of Staffordshire Wildlife Trust said. The donation was made by trust supporter David Aldred.

Plans for the floodplain land include coppicing mature alder trees and managing willow growth to support a greater diversity of plants and wildlife.

Under the trust's ownership, the floodplain will enable the river to flow slower during heavy rainfall and will alleviate flooding downstream.

The reserve's expansion provides public footpaths over the new land, so visitors will be able to explore different trails, the trust said.

"We can restore habitats on a much bigger scale, making more of a difference to the wildlife that relies on these places to live, feed and breed," Sim added.

articles.title: 'Shut up' and listen: Trace Gallagher shares 'unexpected' wisdom learned from being a 'girl dad'
articles.summary: Fox News' Trace Gallagher shares with Fox News Digital the parenting lesson that transformed his bond with his daughters, from a youth soccer moment to learning when to stay silent.
articles.body: For 30 years as a broadcast news anchor, Fox News chief breaking news correspondent Trace Gallagher has built his career on knowing exactly what to say when the camera turns on. Yet when it comes to raising daughters in an increasingly hyper-connected and chaotic world, the veteran newsman says the most powerful tool in a father’s arsenal is paying attention in silence. "These are different people," Gallagher said with a smile about his two daughters, now 25 and 22. "When they have a problem, they don’t really want you to talk to them about their problem. They just want you to hear them about the problem. You need to sit, you need to shut up and you need to listen." TRACE GALLAGHER: COMMON SENSE IS ALIVE IN AMERICA, WE JUST NEED TO LISTEN In an era defined by fast-moving feeds, constant commentary and increasing mental health challenges for young women, fathers often fall into the trap of trying to repair, analyze or lecture their way through their daughters' anxieties, he suggested. Gallagher, who details his parenting journey in his new book "Turns Out They Were Right All Along," admits that overruling his own instincts to speak was an important step in making use of the good advice he's received over a lifetime. "I’m a talkative guy. My career is talking," Gallagher said. "When I was younger with them, I would try to explain what I think." Gallagher figured out that his daughters did want to hear from him. 5 REASONS MORE AMERICANS ARE CUTTING OFF THEIR OWN PARENTS, ACCORDING TO PSYCHOLOGIST What they wanted was to simply be heard. "So then you learn through the years, you just listen, and you nod, and you only jump in when they ask you to jump in," he said. When daughters know their fathers are paying quiet, steady attention without rushing to judge or correct, it fosters a unique sense of security — which Gallagher has learned firsthand. "They want to be heard, they want to get it off their chest," he said. "Instead of screaming and yelling, these girls just want to talk it out. And when requested, they want your advice — but only when requested." CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Although he once dreamed of having an "all-American quarterback" son, Gallagher admitted that having girls is "the greatest thing in the world." "Hey, it's all good. You know, it'll be fine." This active presence extends beyond daily conversations and into how fathers help their daughters build resilience against life's inevitable bumps, he said. Gallagher recalled watching his youngest daughter take a hard fall during a youth soccer match. "I'm looking at her, and she's looking at me, and I said, 'Hey, it's all good. You know, it'll be fine,'" Gallagher recalled. "She scores a goal five minutes later, and she looks over at me.... It is soothing for them to know that somebody is really paying close attention." This contrasts with his mother’s approach when an eight-year-old Gallagher tried to quit football. Instead of making the call for him, his mother — nicknamed "Big Red" — forced him to go to practice and tell the coach himself. By the end of the day, Gallagher was hooked on the game, in part thanks to a coach who likely sensed his hesitation and put him straight to work. "The first couple of weeks, it was just tackling and blocking and calisthenics and jumping jacks and push-ups, and I'm like, "Oh I hate this,'" he recalled. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES "So, I'm sitting in my full pads in my mom's avocado-green recliner ... and I said [to my mother], 'I don't want to play football anymore. I want to quit.' And she said, 'Fine, go quit.' "I walk on to the practice field and the coach looks at me, and he blows the whistle three times, and then he screams at me, 'Gallagher! You're late! Give me five laps.'" Gallagher did as his coach said until he was instructed to get out on the field and stay quiet. And finally, there were footballs. "I fell in love with football and played it through college," he said. "[Coach] saw me coming from a mile away and was not about to let me quit — and my mom knew." TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "And I think that today, kids need to be put in that very same position. If you want to do something, if you want to quit something, you need to do it. You need to fight your own battles." "Listen to people. Hear them out." While talent and teamwork are important for being successful in life, the fortitude to show up every day, despite challenges, is what propels most people forward, he indicated. "You build your career, you build your character and you build your esteem. You build your confidence," he said. "Career, confidence, character." In his new book, Gallagher drives home the message that great guidance is "so valuable to young minds." And some of the most valuable life lessons sometimes come at the most unexpected times from the most unexpected people, he said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "It's so good for young minds and young bodies to get good guidance, but you don't always recognize good guidance," he said. "The best lesson is that wisdom, guidance, advice — it comes at the most unexpected times." "My advice to everybody is listen," he went on. "Listen to people. Hear them out. Sometimes it hits you like a sledgehammer, and sometimes it seeps in, and you don't really understand it for years. So listen." Khloe Quill of Fox News Digital contributed reporting.

articles.title: Pakistan foreign minister dials Iranian counterpart, urges uninterrupted energy supplies and safe passage of ships
articles.summary: Pakistan News: Pakistan’s foreign minister Ishaq Dar on Saturday urged his Iranian counterpart, Abbas Araghchi, that Tehran must ensure “uninterrupted energy supplie.
articles.body: Pakistan’s foreign minister Ishaq Dar on Saturday urged his Iranian counterpart, Abbas Araghchi, that Tehran must ensure “uninterrupted energy supplies” and the “safe and expeditious passage of ships”, amid concerns over disruptions to crucial waterways in the Middle East.Dar, who also serves as Pakistan’s deputy prime minister, held a telephonic conversation with Araghchi to discuss the latest regional developments, according to a statement from Pakistan’s Foreign Office (FO) on X.During the call, Dar “stressed the importance of uninterrupted energy supplies and the safe and expeditious passage of ships, particularly given their implications for developing countries and global supply chains”.He also underscored that “dialogue and diplomacy remain the only viable means to ensure peace and stability in the region”, the FO noted.The two ministers agreed to maintain close cooperation and meet in New York City next week on the sidelines of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly, the foreign office added.The conversation came amid growing concerns over the safety of oil supply routes as tensions escalate around the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb, as well as uncertainty surrounding the United States-Iran war, which began on February 28.The Strait of Hormuz links the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman, while Bab al-Mandeb connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.The Strait of Hormuz has been under a virtual Iranian blockade since March, with Tehran effectively restricting passage through the critical maritime corridor in retaliation for US-Israeli attacks on Iran that triggered the conflict.Meanwhile, Yemen’s Houthi forces, aligned with Tehran, have imposed a de facto blockade on the Bab al-Mandeb Strait since July, seizing key shoreline territory and Mayun Island while specifically targeting Saudi-linked shipping and energy infrastructure.(With PTI inputs)Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Knife attack on Sikh trucker in Wyoming stirs fresh fears in community
articles.summary: While police say the motive is unknown, the attack came after deadly crashes involving Sikh truck drivers led to debate about commercial driver’s licensing requirements.
articles.body: FORT COLLINS, Colo. — The stabbing of a truck driver at a remote Wyoming rest stop had U.S. Sikhs on edge Friday amid rising anti-immigrant vitriol against the community and its truck drivers in particular. The Sikh victim was attacked from behind early Sunday while in a restroom at the Bitter Creek rest stop on Interstate 80 midway between Cheyenne and Salt Lake City, according to court documents. He suffered stabs to the neck and chest and over a dozen other cuts but survived. While police say the motive is unknown, the attack came after deadly crashes involving Sikh truck drivers led to debate about commercial driver’s licensing requirements — sparking hatred toward Sikhs as a group, community leaders said. Anti-Sikh sentiment has been especially severe on truck-driving forums, said one Sikh in the trucking industry, Harsimran Singh, CEO of Gillson Trucking in Stockton, California. “I’ve been here for the last 25-plus years,” Singh said. “I never felt this kind of hate before.” Police were still investigating what prompted the Wyoming attack by a man who left the rest area driving a truck-trailer combination, Sweetwater County Sheriff’s Department spokesperson Jeff Sheaman said. “We have zero motive,” Sheaman said. The victim allegedly told police he was trying to use the restroom when he was attacked from behind. He pushed the attacker, he said, and didn’t see the knife at first, according to the police affidavit filed in the case. Within hours, police arrested Andrew Kris Bzdak in nearby Carbon County, Wyoming. A family at the rest area who heard the attack allegedly followed Bzdak’s truck back onto the highway and tipped off police to help find him, according to the affidavit. Video taken from a truck at the rest area showed the victim walk casually into the restroom, followed by a man police said was Bzdak. Soon after, Bzdak allegedly was recorded running from the restroom, followed by the stumbling, wounded victim who fell at least once, according to the affidavit. Bzdak remained jailed on $1 million bond Friday in Rock Springs, on suspicion of attempted murder, a crime punishable in Wyoming by up to life in prison. An initial appearance was scheduled for Thursday. A phone message left at an address for Bzdak in Catawissa, Pennsylvania, wasn’t immediately returned, nor was a phone message for him at the jail and for his Wyoming public defender, Gary Arnell. Despite no evident motive, the attack was unnerving for Sikhs, who number around 750,000 in the U.S. Many live in California. Sikh men wear beards, uncut hair and turbans, and many work as truck drivers. Advocacy groups estimate at least 150,000 Sikh truck drivers work in the U.S. In August 2025, authorities said a Sikh truck driver’s U-turn on a Florida turnpike caused a crash that killed three people. The crash prompted investigations as well as reports about Sikh truck drivers being harassed. Then last October, a Sikh truck driver accused of being under the influence of drugs caused a fiery crash that killed three people, authorities said. Both drivers were in the U.S. illegally, according to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, which Singh, the trucking CEO, blamed for stirring anti-immigrant hatred with social media posts. One such post, since taken down, showed a dark-skinned man with a beard that read, “Get off our roads, you don’t know how to drive Mr. Singh.” DHS officials have said the post referred specifically to the driver in the Florida crash. But Sikh community representatives pointed out that a large number of Sikhs — well over 100,000 in the U.S. and millions worldwide — have the last name Singh. No matter what motivated the attack, the crime is difficult to separate from racism toward Sikhs, said Jasjit Singh, legal services director for the Sikh community group Jakara Movement and a representative of the victim. “We were making noise about this,” Jasjit Singh said. “That is how the community feels. Until something really bad happens to us, nothing is going to really happen.” The victim was headed home Friday after five days in a Casper hospital and hopes to drive his truck across Wyoming again, Jasjit Singh said. But Harsimran Singh, the trucking CEO, also remained apprehensive. “We are probably going to see more of this,” Harsimran Singh said. “I’m not surprised that it has happened.”

articles.title: Russia reports ‘powerful’ cyberattacks on second day of parliamentary vote
articles.summary: This is Russia’s first election since it invaded Ukraine, and is expected to gauge public support for the ongoing war.
articles.body:
Russian authorities ⁠have reported attacks on ⁠the country’s voting systems and communication lines on the second day of a tightly controlled three-day-long parliamentary election.

Moscow’s electronic voting system was subjected to a powerful cyberattack overnight between Friday and Saturday, and the attack has continued, Interfax news agency reported.

“The Moscow system was under a very powerful attack, literally non-stop, all night long,” Ella Pamfilova, head of the Russian Central Election Commission, told reporters on Saturday morning. “This attack is ongoing almost constantly, and it’s very large-scale and intense, meaning it’s currently targeting Moscow.”

Pamfilova said the electronic voting system is still operating as normal, and did not give details on the nature of the attack or who was responsible.

The election, which will decide all 450 seats in Russia’s lower house, the State Duma, is due to run until 18:00 GMT on Sunday.

The State Duma election is the first since Russia launched its full-scale war on Ukraine in February 2022, and is widely ⁠expected to see the governing pro-Putin United Russia party maintain its dominance in Russia’s tightly controlled political system.

Most antiwar candidates were excluded from the ballot before voting across Russia’s 11 time zones got under way, after the Supreme Court ruled last month that the ‌liberal Yabloko party – which wants a ceasefire in Ukraine – had breached electoral rules, which it has denied.

Russian President Vladimir Putin accused Ukraine on Friday of trying to “hinder” the vote, an accusation to which Kyiv has not responded. Ukraine has called the election farcical.

More than 350 Ukrainian drones targeted the Russian capital on Friday morning, Moscow’s mayor reported.

With the vote potentially offering the Kremlin a measure of the public mood over the invasion, Kyiv has maintained its bid to use air attacks to make Russians feel the impact of the conflict politically, socially, and economically.

Nationwide turnout as of 14:00 local time on Saturday (11:00 GMT) stood at 32.58 percent, according to CEC data cited by state media.

Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova told Russian state news agency TASS that Russians are showing active participation in the ongoing State Duma elections despite physical threats and cyber challenges. She said that the high voter turnout shows people’s united response to the war declared against Russia and its people.

articles.title: 'I knew this was the end of my career': Ajit Doval recalls when his agents were captured by China
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: National security advisor Ajit Doval on Saturday recalled one of the most difficult moments of his early career, when a group of operatives.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: National security advisor Ajit Doval on Saturday recalled one of the most difficult moments of his early career, when a group of operatives sent across the border went missing and were later found to be in Chinese custody.Speaking as the chief guest at the two-day convocation ceremony of IIT Roorkee, NSA Doval said he was deeply worried after receiving no information about the group's whereabouts.He said: “We got no reports of any avalanche or anything. It was a matter of deep worry and concern. But I got a telephone call from the headquarters, and my boss told me, "Have you sent some people across?" I said, "I do not know. They must be coming. They should have come in five or six days, but now it is about ten or eleven days." He said, "They are in Chinese custody now." They were caught by the Chinese and interrogated. Anyway, the Chinese returned them, probably after some talks or negotiations, or a deal must have been struck. So, they returned totally shattered, in shambles. And an inquiry was started. I knew that this was the end of my career. I was still in my twenties, and I had to start a new career. I saw the incident as something very unprofessional.”Doval said an inquiry was later conducted and he was not held responsible for the incident.“Anyway, the inquiry was over. I wasn't found at fault. Probably, I had done everything right. The sketches and the maps that were given to us by the headquarters had some defects and mistakes in them. That is how it happened," the NSA added.He also spoke about the opportunities available to today's younger generation, particularly with rapid advances in technology."You may not be conscious of the fact that in the last 1000 years, you are the luckiest generation, which is going to have so many opportunities. Generations before you were struggling under slavery. They did not have those opportunities which opened up for you. And not only that, things have changed here, but globally things have changed for the better for you... You are coming at an age when technology will be the most important driving factor in any country's or society's growth and progress," Ajit Doval said.The two-day convocation began at IIT Roorkee on Saturday, with degrees set to be awarded to 2,701 students. NSA Doval attended the event as the chief guest.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Police hiring standards matter. But they alone cannot stop abuse
articles.summary: Law enforcement in the US needs high hiring standards. But it also needs reform and trust-building in communities.
articles.body:
During a congressional hearing earlier this week, FBI Director Kash Patel defended changes to the bureau’s hiring standards. His testimony came just two weeks after reports surfaced of loosened hiring standards at another law enforcement agency in the US: Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

As a result, concerns have emerged about a retreat from standards intended to protect the public by offering a baseline of conduct for law enforcement officers. The American public is right to worry. Loose hiring standards can put reckless individuals in positions of power.

But ensuring commitment to higher standards in law enforcement recruitment alone cannot solve the police violence problem in the US.

Research on police misconduct, which has considerably expanded in the wake of Black Lives Matter and related movements, offers useful parameters to guide how we approach the question of hiring standards.

Studies have shown that most cases of use of force are concentrated among a relatively small proportion of officers, at least in the limited departments that track such incidents. That means there are officers who are repeat offenders and have the tendency to engage in such misconduct.

So can risk individuals be identified before they are hired?

One study of more than 12,000 police applicants found that specific responses on pre-employment psychological evaluations were associated with subsequent excessive force complaints and complaints alleging racial misconduct.

However, another study of 642 first-year police officers found that markers for anti-social and borderline behaviour could predict the likelihood of engaging only in certain types of abuse – namely sexual misconduct.

There is also research that suggests abusive policing and officers’ psychological wellbeing may be intertwined, and that the harms of misconduct may extend beyond targeted civilians, possibly even to the offending officers themselves.

In a sample of 137 active-duty US police officers, approximately 11 percent self-reported engaging in abusive policing. Abusive policing was associated with greater PTSD symptoms even after accounting for adverse childhood experiences and workplace trauma.

The implication of all this is that hiring standards based on psychological profiling should neither be dismissed as irrelevant nor treated as a fully reliable way to eliminate all future risk. Standards should be evaluated according to what they actually predict, what they exclude, and what risks arise when they are removed.

But improper selection of law enforcement recruits is only part of the problem.

The US has an exceptionally high rate of police violence compared with other wealthy democracies. For example, the rate of police killings is 33.5 per 10 million in the US, compared with 9.8 in Canada, 1.3 in Germany, and 0.5 in England and Wales.

That cannot plausibly be explained simply by whom we happen to hire. American law enforcement gives officers extraordinary authority to detain, search, use force and, in some circumstances, take a life.

Those powers operate within institutions that have repeatedly struggled with racial bias, unnecessary antagonism of marginalised communities, and abuses of authority. There is also inadequate accountability for law enforcement misconduct, including through qualified immunity and other legal protections that can make it difficult to hold officers personally liable for certain constitutional violations.

The problem, in other words, is not simply that some individuals enter policing who should not. It is also the system into which they enter, and the organisational cultures, incentives, and practices that can shape how they use the power they have been given.

Reducing police misconduct requires system-wide reform, including greater accountability not only for individual officers but for the agencies and institutions responsible for policing.

Effective policing depends in part on public cooperation. Global research across dozens of countries has linked perceived fairness, procedural justice and trust in police to people’s willingness to cooperate with law enforcement.

The credibility of hiring standards can be part of trust-building initiatives, but they must also include broader efforts to strengthen trust and legitimacy among marginalised communities by reducing racial profiling, unnecessary uses of force, and inequitable enforcement of laws.

The challenge is not simply to identify the “wrong” candidates and exclude them, but to build institutions in which selection is accompanied by effective training, supervision, and accountability. Ultimately, the institutions entrusted with extraordinary powers have to be structured to protect the people they serve.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: A hot Atlanta restaurant has a globe-circling menu, regulars lined up at the door, and no building to call its own
articles.summary: A hot Atlanta restaurant has a globe-circling menu, regulars lined up at the door, and no building to call its own
articles.body: It was 4:54 p.m. — six minutes until So So Fed opened for Sunday dinner — and nobody had assembled the siu mai dumplings. Molli Voraotsady, the chef, was up late Saturday night chopping the mushrooms and making the marinade for the pork filling. She’d told the line cooks four hours ago that the siu mai needed to be prepped. Two dozen people were lined up outside, waiting for the restaurant to open. There was no time, or space, to crash out. At 5, as incoming customers poured in, Voraotsady started shaping the dumplings in the open kitchen in front of the bar, while chatting with regulars. Though she looked calm, she would later call that service “one of our hardest.” So So Fed, a Lao-Chinese-American spot that’s one of Atlanta’s buzziest places to eat, has no choice but to pull things together on the fly. The restaurant only exists two nights a week. Pop-up eateries have become more common across the country since the pandemic, thanks to rising costs associated with opening and operating a restaurant. Generally, they look like a chef temporarily taking over a brewery’s unused kitchen or maybe a dinner service held in someone’s apartment. So So Fed, though, has turned its weekly sprint into an endurance event. Since 2023, it has operated inside the space belonging to a Japanese restaurant called OK YAKI, which is open five days a week. Voraotsady and her crew take over when OK YAKI is closed on Sundays and Mondays. Atlanta has become a laboratory of sorts for pop-up service. With funding hard to come by and a lease presenting a daunting commitment, a chef can use a pop-up for proof of concept, building an audience for Texas-style Indian barbecue or modern Polish food — as other Atlanta pop-ups have successfully done — while showing prospective investors they can make those dishes reliably, efficiently and for a profit. OK YAKI itself is a former pop-up that graduated to a fixed, full-time location. Some pop-ups, though, are just fun projects for chefs who don’t plan to build them into full-scale restaurants. So So Fed started as a hobby, while Voraotsady worked full-time managing her husband’s record label and part-time as a server. Voraotsady cooked for friends at her home, then expanded to people in her neighborhood, advertising through flyers and Instagram. She didn’t know what a pop-up was when a friend convinced her to do one at his restaurant in the trendy Poncey-Highland neighborhood. Having never worked in a restaurant kitchen, she thought she could cook the way she did at home. Instead, she found herself frantically shredding papaya to keep up with the incoming papaya salad orders. “I remember feeling despair, like when you feel like there’s no way of digging yourself out of this hole,” she said. Voraotsady sold out within an hour — not because it was busy, but because she hadn’t prepped enough food. “It was fun, but it was awful at the same time,” she said. She tried again, just to prove she could handle it. And then again, to feel that fun-awful rush. And she kept going. Supermarket sweep Today, Voraotsady has a team of line cooks, servers and a recently hired manager. But because So So Fed is a pop-up, meat and produce can’t be directly ordered to the restaurant. There’s no pantry to store extra ingredients. This means Voraotsady’s husband, Ash Jones — who also does the bookkeeping — does the grocery shopping on Sunday mornings. He hit a Costco Business Center when it opens at 9 a.m., buying extra silverware, along with bulk volumes of kosher salt, Kerrygold butter and sugar. From there, he headed to a local Hispanic and Asian grocery store, where So So Fed has a wholesale account and the staff know him as “Mr. So So.” This was a light day, he said — he filled one cart, instead of his usual two, with wonton wrappers, frozen banana leaves, dried mushrooms and coconut milk. He zipped through the aisles, checking items off a list organized in advance by his mental layout of the store; by now he thinks he could map nearly every international grocery store in Atlanta by memory. “Usually I’m like a maniac,” he said. “Just speeding through.” A flatbed at the front awaited with wholesale items including 25 pounds of ground pork, 40 pounds of cubed beef, bags of Thai basil and 30 pounds of fresh papayas. He loaded the haul into a white 2003 Toyota 4Runner, inherited from Voraotsady’s grandmother, and headed home. There, he and Voraotsady meticulously packed rest of the SUV’s interior with a giant steamer, spices and produce, soaked sticky rice, brine for fried chicken, plates, serving dishes, heat lamps, a rice cooker — and even a folding table for a rice station. In a small deli container, they brought their own salt. Local flavor Voraotsady was born in Atlanta. Her mom is from Hong Kong and her dad is from Laos; the name So So Fed is a play on Atlanta’s So So Def record label. Her menu, which changes weekly, is more a self-portrait than a representation of a specific cuisine. On the Fourth of July, she added a burger to the menu without “Asian twists,” as she put it: just lettuce, tomato, cheese, onions, pickles, fries and ketchup. Peach cobbler is a rotating staple, a nod to the Southern woman who was her father’s immigration sponsor. She was inspired by her grandmother, the best Lao cook she knew. Initially, Voraotsady’s only goal was to learn how to cook like her grandmother. But before she could properly study with her, her grandmother died of cancer. Voraotsady taught herself, picking up what she could from YouTube or other family members — often “going off memory or straight vibes” she said, with lots of trial and error. Her grandmother’s influence, she said, comes through in her liberal use of herbs and aromatics. “If a recipe called for some, she’d use like triple that amount,” Voraotsady said. Now, she does the same. On this particular weekend, Voraotsady was starting back up after a three-week break. The menu featured a farmer’s market salad with a Lao-style egg yolk dressing, papaya salad, yellowtail crudo with a yuzu coconut jeow and perilla, vegetable red curry, beef red curry, and the siu mai. There was also a fried chicken plate with jeow som gravy, served with a grilled lemon — a Southern classic reimagined with an Atlanta wink. One pair of regulars, Dhruv Khanna and Simran Singh, said they come in “every week we can.” Today, they’d ordered nearly everything on the menu and brought Singh’s out-of-town parents, who said the couple labeled So So Fed as a “must-do.” “I recognize a lot of people here,” Khanna said. “We’ve seen the food change, people come in and go. It’s a nice little staple of the area.” “It makes it feel like it’s something that’s really intentionally created for the community,” said Lynnea Zhang, who was accompanied by friends, “rather than just any of the 10 million Atlanta restaurants that open up, that are like ‘Oh! Have your cool girls’ brunch here.’” A scramble to open At OK YAKI, as the rest of the crew emptied out the Toyota and set about turning the space into So So Fed, a line cook walked in with even more groceries from another international store. By 12:45 p.m. the stations were set, and Voraotsady went over menu changes and the day’s priorities. Over the next four hours, ’90s hip-hop and R&B played as cooks sliced yellowtail for crudo, shredded papaya and mixed dumpling filling. The simmering curry filled the air with the aroma of coconut milk and red curry paste, while chicken thighs were wet brined in a dining room booth. In just one two-day workweek at So So Fed, one line cook said, they clock 30 hours. The cook said they spend the rest of their time “trying to be a drummer.” There are restaurants where line cooks hardly see their presiding chefs. This is not one of them. Voraotsady — whose own focus was a blueberry compote for ube sugar toast — made sure the curry simmered on low enough heat, double-checked the sizes of chopped vegetables, and occasionally reminded the staff to clean as they went and not to get distracted on their phones. Most of the front-of-house staff clocked in around 4 p.m. The floors were swept, chairs were set up, flowers from a local farm decorated the tables. Customers accidentally wandered in, thinking the restaurant was already open. Then it was time for the final steps: putting up the So So Fed sign, shoving red peppers into the walk-in, discovering a lack of batteries in the timer for the siu mai. And then — in a brief panic — discovering there were no siu mai ready to go, either. A whole restaurant to go The second day’s work began with a line cook, in charge of a new round of grocery shopping, discovering that the “check engine” light in his car was on. Another cook took over the shopping, and a third cook had to bring him to the restaurant — meaning three out of four line cooks would get in late. “There’s always something,” Voraotsady said. “There’s never a smooth shift.” Chaos allowed for moments of community. The manager ran to a small Asian market in search of more banana leaves. At the mention of Voraotsady and So So Fed, the owner — who happened to be Lao — agreed to sell all the banana leaves she had, even though she had saved them for a different restaurant. It all worked out, and So So Fed made it to 11 p.m. The last lingering customers left, and the dismantling began. Leftover produce, meat and pantry items were divided into items that could be used next week and what could go home with staff. One cook took yellowtail scraps for his cats. The leftover curry and brined chicken thighs were handed out, as were the flowers from the tables. Surfaces were scrubbed down, while dishes were washed and categorized into what Voraotsady had brought and what belonged to OK YAKI. They’d hear about it if anything got left behind, Voraotsady said, and she didn’t want to drive 30 minutes to pick up a spoon. A pop-up crew doesn’t have the luxury of slacking off the cleaning at close for the next day’s shift to complain about. As guests, the staff has to leave the space even cleaner than they found it. It takes a lot of trust for a business owner to open their space up to a stranger. So So Fed’s manager used to work in the Bay Area, and said the restaurant-sharing deal would never have worked there. There’s a willingness to help each other out in Atlanta, she said. By 2 a.m., cleanup was completed and So So Fed was repacked into the 4Runner. Voraotsady didn’t seem to have sat down once during the night. The team shared a round of shots — Voraotsady chose Fernet — and cheered. Outside, some lit cigarettes and lingered under the awning, relaxed for the first time in 48 hours. Until recently, there were days where So So Fed only broke even. Lately, though, they’ve been profitably busy — maybe even too busy. But Voraotsady feels like she finally knows how to run a restaurant now, with consistent recipes and steady marketing. It’s a huge jump for someone who started by panic-shredding papaya to order. Back home, her husband would unload the car, and she’d be asleep by 4 a.m. In six days, she’d do it all over again.
